trial_name: STOPAH — Prednisolone or Pentoxifylline for Alcoholic Hepatitis (2015)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Thursz MR, Richardson P, Allison M, et al. Prednisolone or Pentoxifylline for Alcoholic Hepatitis. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(17):1619-1628.
trial_type: RCT — pragmatic, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2x2 factorial
one_liner: In severe alcoholic hepatitis, pentoxifylline provides no survival benefit, while prednisolone yields only a non-significant trend toward reduced 28-day mortality that is lost by 90 days and accompanied by increased serious infections.

pico.population: Hospitalised adults with severe alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function >=32, serum bilirubin >80 umol/L, recent heavy alcohol intake).
pico.intervention: Prednisolone 40 mg once daily, pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily, or both for 28 days.
pico.outcome: Primary: 28-day all-cause mortality; Secondary: 90-day and 1-year death or liver transplantation, serious infections, acute kidney injury.

background.existing_knowledge: Severe alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function >=32) carries a historical 1-month mortality of 20-30% and 6-month mortality of 30-40%. Prednisolone was widely used despite conflicting evidence and infection concerns; pentoxifylline was adopted based on small trials suggesting reduced hepatorenal syndrome.
background.knowledge_gap: Conflicting meta-analyses and practice variation created uncertainty regarding whether prednisolone, pentoxifylline, or combination therapy improves survival in severe alcoholic hepatitis.
background.hypothesis: A 28-day regimen of prednisolone and/or pentoxifylline reduces 28-day, 90-day, and 1-year mortality without additive adverse interactions.

methods.design: Pragmatic, multicenter, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2x2 factorial trial conducted across 65 UK hospitals (January 2011 to February 2014).
methods.setting: 65 UK hospitals (inpatient medical and hepatology wards, not restricted to ICU).

inclusion: Clinical diagnosis of severe alcoholic hepatitis
Average alcohol intake >80 g/day for men or >60 g/day for women
Recent onset of jaundice (<= 3 months) and recent alcohol excess (<= 2 months before admission)
exclusion: Other causes of chronic or acute liver disease
Serum AST >500 IU/L or ALT >300 IU/L

Uncontrolled active gastrointestinal bleeding, untreated sepsis, severe renal failure (creatinine >500 umol/L or renal replacement therapy), or vasopressor support unless stabilised within the first 7 days of admission

methods.intervention: Prednisolone 40 mg orally once daily for 28 days, pentoxifylline 400 mg orally three times daily for 28 days, or both.
methods.comparison: Matched placebos for each agent permitting double-blind 2x2 factorial allocation, plus standard supportive care and nutritional support at clinician discretion.
methods.blinding: Double-blind for participants, clinicians, and investigators using identical placebo tablets/capsules.
methods.sample_size_power: Target sample size was 1,200 to detect an absolute mortality reduction from 30% to 21% (513 per main-effect group). Enrolled 1,103 due to funding limitations.
secondary_outcomes: Death or liver transplantation at 90 days
Death or liver transplantation at 1 year
Incidence of serious infections and acute kidney injury within 28 days
methods.follow_up: 28 days for primary endpoint; 90 days and 1 year for secondary endpoints (long-term follow-up truncated early for later recruits).

headline_bullets: Trial stopped early at 1,103 participants due to funding constraints.
Pentoxifylline conferred no mortality benefit at 28 days (16% vs 16%), 90 days, or 1 year.

Prednisolone showed a non-significant trend toward reduced 28-day mortality in the primary model (14% vs 18%; OR 0.72; p=0.06), which reached significance in a prespecified adjusted model (OR 0.61; p=0.02).
Prednisolone mortality benefit was absent at 90 days (30% vs 29%) and 1 year (57% vs 56%), and it significantly increased serious infections (13% vs 7%).

outcomes_table.note: Primary endpoint; unadjusted factorial logistic regression; no drug interaction (p=0.41)
Primary endpoint main effect for pentoxifylline
Adjusted for baseline age, encephalopathy, WBC, PT ratio, bilirubin, creatinine, urea

outcomes_table.outcome: 90-day death or liver transplant (Prednisolone main effect)
outcomes_table.note: Incomplete follow-up due to early trial termination

outcomes_table.outcome: 90-day death or liver transplant (Pentoxifylline main effect)
outcomes_table.note: No late mortality or transplantation signal

outcomes_table.outcome: 1-year death or liver transplant (Prednisolone main effect)
1-year death or liver transplant (Pentoxifylline main effect)
Serious infections within 28 days (Prednisolone main effect)
outcomes_table.note: Significant increase in serious infection with steroids

outcomes_table.outcome: Lung infections within 28 days (Prednisolone main effect)
Acute kidney injury within 28 days (Pentoxifylline main effect)
outcomes_table.note: No clinical signal for renal protection

safety: Prednisolone significantly increased serious infections within 28 days (13% [71/547] vs 7% [38/545], p=0.002; absolute difference 6%).
Prednisolone significantly increased lung infections within 28 days (7% [37/547] vs 3% [17/545], p=0.007; absolute difference 4%).
Pentoxifylline failed to show a clinically meaningful reduction in acute kidney injury within 28 days (2% [9/546] vs 3% [14/546]).

domains.notes: Central computer-generated randomisation with permuted blocks of 4, stratified by geography and baseline risk category.
Double-blinded using matched identical placebos for both agents; objective primary endpoint (all-cause mortality).

ITT primary analysis on 1,053/1,103 participants (95.5% complete). Follow-up denominators dropped to 968 at 90 days (5% lost, 3% withdrawn, 4% truncated) and 747 at 1 year (8% lost, 4% withdrawn, 20% truncated) due to early study termination.
Biological separation confirmed by steroid-associated infection risk; crossovers not reported.
Well-balanced groups: mean Discriminant Function 60.7–65.6, MELD 20.7–21.5, mean time to treatment 6.1–6.7 days, baseline sepsis 8–11%, baseline GI bleeding 5–8%, baseline renal failure <0.5%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong for 28-day primary mortality outcomes, but moderate-to-low for 90-day and 1-year outcomes due to early termination and loss of follow-up.

domains.notes: Large real-world UK cohort with clinical entry criteria (mean bilirubin 17.6 mg/dL, DF 62.6, MELD 21.2) representing typical medical/hepatology ward admissions.
Exclusion or stabilization requirement for active bleeding, untreated sepsis, vasopressors, or severe acute kidney injury limits direct applicability to unstable ICU patients in multi-organ failure.

external_validity.verdict: Good applicability to hospitalised, non-critically ill or stabilised patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis, but limited for patients with unmanaged sepsis, septic shock, or multi-organ failure.

strengths: Largest double-blind placebo-controlled RCT in severe alcoholic hepatitis.
Factorial 2x2 design enabled efficient assessment of individual drugs and their interaction.
Pragmatic multicenter recruitment across 65 hospitals mirrors everyday practice.
High completeness of follow-up (95.5%) for the primary 28-day endpoint.
limitations: Early termination (1,103 of 1,200 planned) reduced statistical power.
Substantial missing data at 90 days and 1 year due to early follow-up truncation.
Clinical diagnosis without mandatory liver biopsy introduces potential diagnostic misclassification.
Exclusion/stabilization criteria limit applicability to the most unstable ICU phenotypes.

critical_appraisal.summary: STOPAH is a landmark pragmatic trial demonstrating that pentoxifylline provides no clinical benefit and that prednisolone offers at best a non-significant, short-term survival trend that is accompanied by increased infection risk and absent long-term survival gains.
strengths: Pragmatic enrolment across 65 centers ensuring high clinical relevance.
weaknesses: Unpowered long-term secondary outcomes due to early trial closure.

sections.authors_conclusion: Pentoxifylline did not improve survival in severe alcoholic hepatitis. Prednisolone was associated with a trend toward reduced 28-day mortality that did not reach statistical significance, with no survival improvement at 90 days or 1 year.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Pentoxifylline should be abandoned for severe alcoholic hepatitis. Prednisolone should be used selectively for short-term benefit in patients screened for infection, with mandatory early response assessment (e.g., day 7 Lille score) to stop non-beneficial steroids.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Hospitalised patients with clinical severe alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey DF >= 32) without active untreated infection or gastrointestinal bleeding.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean corticosteroids confer durable 90-day or 1-year survival benefits or that they are safe in the presence of active untreated infection.
implementation_caveats: Screen and monitor rigorously for pulmonary and serious infections before and during steroid therapy.
Remove pentoxifylline from institutional orders and treatment protocols.
Re-evaluate treatment response early at day 7 to stop steroids in non-responders.

controversies.notes: Omitting mandatory liver biopsy raised concerns about diagnostic noise diluting treatment response, though trialists noted non-biopsy strategies reflect real-world clinical care.

controversies.topic: Primary unadjusted vs secondary adjusted prednisolone results
controversies.notes: Primary unadjusted analysis missed significance (p=0.06), whereas secondary multivariable adjustment was significant (OR 0.61; p=0.02), prompting debate on whether steroids provide a true modest short-term benefit.
Abrupt steroid discontinuation at 28 days was postulated to cause rebound inflammation, contributing to the loss of survival benefit by 90 days.

context_related_trials.relation: Shifted clinical focus toward combining corticosteroids with antioxidant/organ-protective strategies rather than pentoxifylline.

unresolved_questions: Optimal management for non-responders to early corticosteroid therapy.
Efficacy and safety of corticosteroid therapy in critically ill ICU patients with organ failure requiring vasopressors or renal support.
Impact of combining early anti-inflammatory therapy with targeted infection prophylaxis or antioxidant agents.

numbers_to_remember: Prednisolone 28-day mortality: 14% vs 18% (OR 0.72, p=0.06; adjusted OR 0.61, p=0.02)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Pentoxifylline is ineffective in severe alcoholic hepatitis, while prednisolone provides at best a modest 28-day mortality reduction offset by doubled infection risk and no 90-day survival benefit.
